title: Architecture & Standards — Integrated Guidelines and ADRs
author: Marina Patel
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and engineering standards across API, coding, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It also summarizes active Decision Records (ADRs) relevant to implementing and enforcing these standards. The goal is a single reference for design, reviews, and audits; teams should reference the relevant subsection for day-to-day decisions.

Audience
- Engineering teams (serving runtime, infra, platform, developer experience)
- Product and security reviewers
- SRE and performance engineers

Principles
1. Developer-first: APIs and infra should be predictable, discoverable, and easy to integrate.
2. Production-first: defaults should favor reliability, observability, and cost-awareness.
3. Backwards-compatible evolution: prefer additive changes and explicit deprecation windows.
4. Measure and validate: every standard must have measurable tests (benchmarks, SLOs, lint/test gates).

1) API Standards
Purpose: Ensure consistent client experience (hosted, dedicated, private) and reduce integration errors.

Key rules:
- Surface: REST+JSON primary surface for internal services; public-facing SDKs wrap the REST API.
- Resource naming: kebab-case for endpoints (e.g., /v1/models, /v1/inference/stream).
- Versioning: Use major version in path (/v1/). Breaking changes must follow ADR process and provide 90-day deprecation prior to removal for public endpoints.
- Idempotency: All mutating operations must accept an optional idempotency_key header.
- Paging: Use cursor-based paging with `next_cursor` token for large result sets.
- Pagination defaults: default page_size=50, max_page_size=1000 for list endpoints.
- Rate limiting: 429 response with `Retry-After` header; use per-route and per-customer quotas (see pricing-and-packaging docs).
- Error model: Standard error envelope: {"code": "string", "message": "string", "details": [string]}. Use 4xx for client, 5xx for server. Include trace_id in response headers (X-Trace-Id).
- Streaming: Server-Sent Events (SSE) or chunked JSON for streaming responses; include `event: token` boundary for parsing.

API Example (curl):
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/inference \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"open-redwood-v1", "input":"Hello world"}'

Acceptance criteria for API work:
- OpenAPI spec updated and published for the endpoint.
- Integration tests exercising happy and error paths.
- Backwards-compatibility checklist completed if changing a public route.

2) Coding Standards

Languages & tooling:
- Primary backend languages: Go (for performance-sensitive infra), Python (model tooling & evals), and TypeScript (frontend & API gateway).
- Linting: golangci-lint for Go, ruff/black/isort for Python, ESLint/Prettier for TypeScript.
- Static typing: enable go vet and `--strict` mypy/pyright rules on test/CI for Python and TypeScript.
- Formatting: apply automatic formatters in pre-commit to reduce style PR churn.

Testing:
- Unit tests: target 80% coverage on critical path modules; aim for >90% on libraries.
- Integration tests: run against local emulators or test clusters (see eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build).
- Performance tests: include microbenchmarks for RPCs and hot-path functions.
- Contract tests: API schema contract tests between client and service.

Code review rules:
- Two reviewers minimum for public-facing services; at least one reviewer outside the authoring team for cross-cutting changes.
- PRs must include a short design rationale and link to ADR if applicable.

3) Infrastructure Standards

IaC and accounts:
- All cloud resources must be managed via Terraform modules in the `infra` monorepo. No manual changes in production accounts.
- Environment separation: dev, staging, prod in separate accounts/projects with explicit IAM boundary.
- GitOps: apply changes via merge to main -> CI pipeline -> plan + manual or automated apply per target environment.

Networking & security:
- Default deny egress/ingress for internal services; open minimum required ports.
- Private subnets for GPU nodes and model-serving backends; public NAT for egress where necessary.
- KMS for secrets and encryption-at-rest; do not store plaintext secrets in Git.

Capacity & scaling:
- GPU fleet sizing: reserve levers for burst vs reserved Dedicated capacity (see eng-sre/capacity-planning).
- Autoscaling policy: horizontal pod autoscaler (HPA) with CPU/GPU utilization and custom metrics (queue depth, in-flight requests).

4) Model-serving Standards

Packaging & deployment:
- Model bundle format: standardized tar.gz containing model weights, config.yaml (schema below), and a minimal load-test manifest.
- Supported formats: PyTorch (fp16/fp32), ONNX, and quantized artifacts (4/8-bit using supported runtime).
- Model manifest (config.yaml) fields (required):
  - model_name: string
  - version: semver string
  - architecture: string (e.g., gpt-2, llama-xxx)
  - input_tokens: max_input_tokens (int)
  - quantization_profile: string (recommended profile id)
  - recommended_batch_size: int

Runtime behavior:
- KV-cache lifecycle: cache per-model-version and evict LRU by default; persistent on warmup where possible.
- Quantization: follow approved profiles in confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles; runtime must validate post-quantization accuracy using a short eval set before serving traffic.
- Rollouts: Canary (5%) -> Ramp (25%/50%) -> Full with health checks and rollback on error rate >3x baseline or latency regressions >30% at p95.

Fallbacks & compatibility:
- Model variants: each model must publish compatible fallbacks (smaller sizes or quantized versions). Smart routing may fallback to a compatible variant automatically when capacity constrained.

5) Observability Standards

Metrics:
- Metric naming: use prometheus naming conventions with service prefix (e.g., inference_request_total, inference_latency_seconds_bucket).
- Required metrics per service: request_count, error_count (4xx/5xx), latency_histogram (p50/p90/p95/p99), active_requests, queue_depth, batch_size_mean.
- Cardinality: limit label cardinality; avoid unbounded labels (user_id should not be a metric label).

Tracing & Logs:
- Traces: use OpenTelemetry tracing with X-Trace-Id propagated across RPC boundaries. Sample rate: 1% by default, increase to 100% for canary rollouts.
- Logs: structured JSON logs, include trace_id and request_id. Log retention: 90 days for production error logs; 30 days for debug-level logs (configurable with add-on).

Dashboards & Alerts:
- Standard dashboards: per-service overview (traffic, error rate, latency), per-model serving dashboard (throughput, batch sizes, p95 latency), and a cross-service dependency map.
- SLOs and alerts: define SLOs as code in the `slo` repo with alerting rules in the `monitoring` repo.

6) Performance Standards

SLOs & targets (examples):
- Availability: 99.95% uptime for hosted control plane, 99.9% for dedicated model-serving clusters.
- Latency (inference, short inputs <512 tokens): p50 < 60ms, p95 < 220ms, p99 < 600ms for Dedicated / Hosted with reserved capacity. For cold-start or private on-prem, document expected higher latencies in model manifest.
- Throughput: measurement per-GPU in requests/sec and tokens/sec for each model; every model must publish a measured baseline in benchmarking-and-perf-suite.

Benchmarking & validation:
- Benchmark harness: use eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite to produce reproducible perf numbers (hardware, batch sizes, sequence length).
- Regression testing: automated perf regression job on main that compares to baseline; failures open a perf-incident if >10% degradation at p95 for a canonical set.

7) Decision Records (ADRs) Summary

This section lists key architecture decisions and links to full ADRs. Each ADR includes context, decision, alternatives considered, and rollout plan.

Active ADRs (examples):
- ADR-2025-07: Default inference protocol: HTTP/1.1 + JSON over gRPC for internal high-throughput paths. (owner: Runtime)
- ADR-2025-11: Use OpenTelemetry as standard tracing (owner: Observability)
- ADR-2026-01: Quantization profiles and accuracy validation gates (owner: Applied ML)
- ADR-2026-03: API versioning and deprecation policy (owner: API Standards)

ADR Template (use when authoring new ADRs):
1) Title
2) Status (proposed | accepted | superseded)
3) Context and problem statement
4) Decision
5) Rationale & alternatives considered
6) Consequences & migration plan
7) Owners and reviewers

Operationalizing and Ownership
- Ownership: each service/team must declare a documented OWNER (team@redwood.ai) in the service README and in the infra repo.
- Reviews: architecture changes that cross team boundaries require a documented ADR and at least two reviewers from impacted teams.
- Enforcement: CI gates (lint/tests/slo checks) are required prior to merging to main for services in production.

Onboarding checklist for new services
1. Create service README with owner, purpose, and diagrams.
2. Add service to monitoring with basic dashboard and alert rules (templates provided).
3. Publish OpenAPI/asyncAPI spec if exposing an API.
4. Add IaC module and run plan in staging account.
5. Run a perf microbenchmark and publish results to benchmarking tracker.

Appendix: Example model config.yaml
model_name: open-redwood-v1
version: 1.2.0
architecture: autoregressive-gpt
max_input_tokens: 4096
quantization_profile: q4_0_recommended
recommended_batch_size: 8
owner: team-inference

Appendix: ADR index links
- Full ADRs are stored under confluence/architecture-and-standards and the `adrs` folder in the eng repo; search for prefix `ADR-YYYY-##`.

Contact / questions
- For questions about these standards, file a PR or open an issue in the `architecture-standards` repo and tag the owners. Primary contact: Marina Patel (marina@redwood.ai).
